faq.title: Questions that decide whether we should work together.
faq.subtitle: Straight answers before either side spends time on a proposal.

cta.btn: Ask it on a free call

faq.q1: Will you build my Uber for X?
faq.a1: Maybe. But on the first call we'll ask which side you can get 100 of by hand, without ads. If there's no answer, the product isn't ready and we'll say so instead of taking the money.
faq.a2: Because a fourth would be a claim we can't back with work yet – we're building our first agritech platform now and we'll say so plainly until it ships. We build platforms where participants have to find and trust each other. That shape repeats across marketplaces, clubs and logistics. Outside it we'd be guessing on your budget.
faq.q3: How much does a platform cost?
faq.a3: It depends on the trust model, number of participant roles and operational tooling. We'll give you a rough budget range on the first call and a fixed price after scope. If a prototype is the smarter first step, we'll say so.
faq.q4: Can I hire you for just design, or just development?
faq.a4: Yes. Design-only, build-only, or marketing-only all work. We'll scope it accordingly.
faq.q5: Do you work with existing codebases?
faq.a5: Yes. We'll audit first and give you an honest verdict, including "rewrite" or "keep your current team."
faq.q6: What does working together look like?
faq.a6: Discovery → design → build → launch. One-week sprints, a demo every sprint. You always know what shipped and what's next.
faq.a7: Retainers for ongoing development and iteration. Most clients stay – but the first version is the one that decides whether there's anything to iterate on.
faq.a8: Book the free call or send the form. We reply within 24 hours with relevant cases and an honest read on fit.

hero.title: Marketplace development for platforms that start empty
hero.subtitle: Matching, payments and disputes are easy to put in a spec and hard to get right. We have taken five platforms through a launch day where neither side existed yet.

problem.title: A marketplace is not a catalogue with a checkout.
paragraphs: The part everyone quotes for is listings, search and payment. That part is well understood, and it is not where marketplaces die. They die in month two, when one side has signed up, the other has not, and nothing in the product gives either a reason to come back.

The mechanics that fix that – who gets verified, what a profile has to prove before a stranger transacts with it, what happens when a booking goes wrong at 9pm on a Saturday – get scoped as phase two. By phase two the platform is already empty and the team is arguing about ads.
We design for the empty state first. The opening question is not what you want built. It is who shows up on day one, and why they stay while the other side is still thin.

included.title: What a marketplace build actually includes
included.subtitle: Not a feature list. The parts that decide whether the platform survives its first year.

items.title: Two-sided onboarding
items.body: Separate flows for supply and demand, each of which has to be usable while the other side is still empty. This is the part that gets designed last and matters most.

items.title: Verification and trust states
items.body: Identity checks, reputation, reviews, and the states in between – pending, limited, trusted, suspended. In a marketplace this is not compliance work, it is the product.

items.title: Payments, payouts and refunds
items.body: Escrow or direct, split payments, partial refunds, payout schedules, and VAT handling for sellers across EU borders. Refunds are where most integrations turn out to be half-built.

items.title: Matching and search
items.body: Ranking that works with fifty listings, not just fifty thousand. Geography, availability and relevance, tuned for a thin catalogue rather than a mature one.

items.title: Disputes and moderation
items.body: Moderation queues, dispute flows, evidence handling, and a manual override on every automated decision. Your ops team will need all four in the first month.

items.title: Admin tooling
items.body: User impersonation, refunds, roles and permissions, audit log. It never appears in a portfolio and it is the difference between a platform you can run and one you can only demo.

process.title: How the build runs
process.subtitle: Weekly demos against working software. No status decks.

steps.title: Cold-start audit
steps.body: Ninety minutes on who joins first and why they stay. Sometimes the honest answer is that you do not need a platform yet, and we will say so.

steps.title: Flows before pixels
steps.body: User flows, edge cases and trust states mapped end to end, including what every screen looks like with no data in it. Most projects are won or lost here.

steps.title: Build in one-week sprints
steps.body: Working staging environment from the first sprint, demo every week. Admin tooling ships with each feature rather than being promised for later.

steps.title: Launch and the first ninety days
steps.body: Instrumentation, a moderation playbook your team can actually operate, and the changes the first real users force. We stay through that part.

items.q: What drives the cost of a marketplace build?
items.a: Four things, in order: how many verification and trust states the product needs, how complex the money flow is (escrow, splits, cross-border VAT), how much moderation and dispute handling your category requires, and how much admin tooling your ops team needs on day one. items.a: Yes. Most marketplaces eventually need at least one native app, usually for the supply side. We will also tell you when a responsive web app buys you another six months and the app can wait.

hero.title: P2P platform development, where trust is the product
hero.subtitle: Two strangers, one item, and real money moving between them. The hard part is not the listing page – it is everything that happens when the handover goes wrong.

problem.title: A P2P product is a marketplace with the safety net removed.
paragraphs: In a managed marketplace the operator stands behind the transaction. In a peer-to-peer product the two users carry the risk themselves, which means every mechanic that makes them feel safe is load-bearing. Take it out and the listings never convert.

That changes what has to exist on day one. Identity that is strong enough for a stranger to hand over a drill, a car or an apartment key. Deposits that can be held and released without a support ticket. Evidence capture at handover, because damage claims are not an edge case, they are a weekly occurrence.

We have built this twice in anger – an item-sharing platform with real logistics, and an on-demand service product where the person arriving at your door is not an employee. Most of the work is in the states nobody demos.

included.title: What a P2P build has to cover
included.subtitle: The mechanics that let two strangers transact without you in the middle of every exchange.

items.title: Identity and verification
items.body: Document checks, phone and email verification, selfie match where the category needs it, and a graded trust model rather than a single verified badge.

items.title: Deposits and held funds
items.body: Authorisations, deposits, release rules and partial captures for damage. The flow has to work without a human approving every release, and still be reversible when it goes wrong.

items.title: Handover and evidence
items.body: Photo capture at pickup and return, timestamped condition records, and a shared trail both sides can see. This is what turns a dispute from an argument into a decision.

items.title: Reputation that means something
items.body: Two-sided reviews that cannot be gamed by one party, cancellation records, and a reputation that survives a user making one new account.

items.title: Disputes and resolution
items.body: Structured claims, evidence review, partial outcomes, and an escalation path. Plus the admin side of it, because someone on your team resolves these every week.

items.title: Logistics where it applies
items.body: Pickup windows, delivery handoff, no-show handling and the awkward middle state where an item is in transit and nobody is responsible for it.

process.title: How the build runs
process.subtitle: Trust mechanics first, because everything else depends on them.

steps.title: Risk and trust mapping
steps.body: What can go wrong between two users in your category, how often, and what the product does in each case. This drives the whole build.

steps.title: Flows before pixels
steps.body: Every trust state drawn end to end: unverified, pending, limited, trusted, suspended, in dispute. Including what each screen shows when the catalogue is nearly empty.

steps.title: Build in one-week sprints
steps.body: Verification, money movement and dispute handling ship early rather than last, because they change the data model and you do not want to retrofit them.

steps.title: Launch and first disputes
steps.body: The first real claims teach you more than the research did. We stay through them and tune the rules with your ops team.

faq.title: Questions we get before a P2P build

items.q: What is the difference between a P2P platform and a marketplace?
items.a: A marketplace can operate with a managed supply side and the operator absorbing risk. A peer-to-peer product puts two private users on either end, so identity, deposits and dispute resolution move from back-office concerns to core product. We wrote this up in detail on the blog.

items.q: How long does a P2P platform take to build?
items.a: Four to five months for a first version that handles verification, held funds and disputes properly. It is longer than a managed marketplace because the trust layer cannot be deferred – it shapes the data model.

items.q: Do we need identity verification from day one?
items.a: Almost always, in some form. The strength should match what is being exchanged: a phone number is enough for a low-value swap, a document check is not optional when someone hands over car keys. We will help you pick the weakest verification your category tolerates, because every extra step costs you supply.

items.q: How do you handle damage and disputes?
items.a: Evidence first: timestamped condition records at handover from both sides. Then a structured claim with partial outcomes, not a binary refund, and a resolution queue your team can work through. The product should make most disputes decidable without a phone call.

items.q: Can you integrate deposits with our existing payment provider?
items.a: Usually. Deposits, authorisations and partial captures are supported by the major providers, with real differences in how long an authorisation holds and how partial captures behave. We check that against your category before committing to one.

items.q: What if we are not sure a P2P model is right?
items.a: Then that is the first thing to settle. Some products are better as a managed service with suppliers you control, at least for the first year. We would rather lose the project on that call than watch it stall at month five.

hero.title: MVP development for two-sided products

problem.title: Most MVPs test the wrong thing.
paragraphs: Teams build a thin version of every feature and launch it. What comes back is a vague signal: some signups, little usage, no clarity on why. The scope was decided by what was easy to cut rather than by what was genuinely uncertain.

For a two-sided product the uncertainty is nearly always on one side. Can we get supply without demand. Will anyone verify themselves before there is anything to transact. Will the second side come back a week later. A good MVP is shaped around that question and ruthless about everything else.

We also take the opposite position often enough to mention it: sometimes the first version should not be software. A spreadsheet, a group chat and a person doing the matching by hand will answer the question faster and cheaper, and we will tell you when that is the case.

faq.title: Questions we get before a mobile build

items.q: Native, cross-platform or web app?
items.a: Cross-platform covers most marketplace and on-demand products, including ours. Go native when you need sustained background location, deep hardware access or platform-specific performance. Stay on web when the product is occasional-use and you want to ship changes daily. We wrote a longer comparison on the blog.

items.q: How long does a mobile app take to build?
items.a: Two to four months for a first version tied to an existing backend, longer when the platform behind it is being built at the same time. Store review adds days, not weeks, once the account setup is done early.

items.q: Do we need two apps, one for customers and one for workers?
items.a: If the people doing the work are not your employees, usually yes – their needs are different enough that one app serves neither well. Sometimes the right answer is a customer app plus a mobile web tool for the workers, which is cheaper and we will say when it fits.

items.q: What drives the cost of a mobile build?
items.a: Offline requirements, payments, real-time tracking and the number of distinct user roles. Store presence itself is a small fixed cost; the variable is how much of the product has to keep working when the network does not.

items.q: Can you take over an existing app?
items.a: Yes, after an audit. We will tell you honestly whether the codebase is worth continuing or whether the remaining work is cheaper on a fresh foundation. We have recommended both.

items.q: Who owns the store accounts?
items.a: You do. Apps are published under your developer accounts, with your certificates, so you are never locked to us for a release.

problem.title: The site ends where the work begins.
paragraphs: Most service businesses already have a website. It describes the service, shows a phone number and a contact form, and that is where it stops. Everything that actually runs the business happens after that: someone answers the phone, writes the order into a chat, and matches it to whoever is free.

That gap costs in three ways at once. Customers who call outside working hours go elsewhere. Orders live in WhatsApp and a spreadsheet, so nobody can tell you what last month looked like. And aggregators take a cut of every booking precisely because they own the part your site does not do.

So the brief is not really a website. It is a site that completes a booking by itself, a place clients come back to, and a panel your team runs the day on. Those three are one system, and building them separately is how they drift apart.

faq.title: Questions we get before a booking build

items.q: We already have a website. Do we start over?
items.a: Usually not. If the current site brings in traffic and the content is fine, we add the booking flow and the portal to it and leave the marketing pages alone. A rebuild is worth it when the site cannot be extended or when it loses people before they reach the form.

items.q: How long until bookings come through the site?
items.a: Three to five weeks for the booking flow on an existing site, longer when the site is being rebuilt at the same time. We ship that part first on purpose, so the project starts paying before the apps are done.

items.q: Do we need a mobile app?
items.a: Clients usually do not – a fast mobile site beats an app they have to install first. The people doing the work often do, because they are outside with one hand free. We will tell you when a mobile web tool is enough for the crew and saves you an app.

items.q: What does it cost?
items.a: It depends on how many services and rules the booking has to express, whether payments are online, and whether the team side is a web tool or a native app. We write out what is in scope and what is not before you sign – that is usually where quotes diverge.

items.q: Can it work with the system we already use?
items.a: Usually yes. Calendars, accounting and messaging have workable APIs. If something critical has none, we will say so on the first call rather than discover it in month three.

items.q: Who owns it?
items.a: You do, from the first commit, in your repositories and your accounts. We work from our Poznań entity on EU contracts, so data and IP stay inside the EU.
